answer.text: It rises, because removing CO2 lowers carbonic acid
answer.line: Breathing out CO2 pulls the carbonic acid chain back toward CO2. That uses up H^+, so the blood turns less acidic.

steps: Write the chain first. CO2 and water make carbonic acid, which splits into H^+ and HCO3^-. Each step runs both ways.
Pull out CO2. Hyperventilating removes it, so the chain shifts back toward CO2 to replace it.
That shift uses up H^+ and carbonic acid. Fewer H^+ means a higher pH: respiratory alkalosis.

choices.text: It falls, because less bicarbonate is made
choices.note: Bicarbonate does dip a little as the chain shifts back. But H^+ is used up too, so the pH climbs.

choices.text: It does not change, because blood is buffered
choices.note: A buffer softens added acid or base. Here the acid's own source, CO2, is leaving, and that moves the pH.

choices.text: It rises, because hyperventilating adds extra bicarbonate to the blood
choices.note: The pH does rise, but not from added bicarbonate. Bicarbonate drops a little; the rise comes from H^+ being used up.

choices.text: It falls, because CO2 is a base
choices.note: CO2 makes carbonic acid in water, so it acts as an acid. Losing an acid makes the blood less acidic.

choices.text: It rises, because removing CO2 lowers carbonic acid
choices.note: Less CO2, less carbonic acid, less H^+: pH up.

lockIt: Remove a species and the equilibrium shifts to make more of it. Blowing off CO2 raises blood pH.

visual.alt: The carbonic acid chain: CO2 and water, then carbonic acid, then hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, linked by equilibrium arrows. An arrow lifts CO2 out of the first box, breathed out, and a long arrow under the chain points left. Below: carbonic acid falls and, outlined, hydrogen ion used up, pH rises.
visual.caption: Start where CO2 leaves, then follow the long arrow left. Everything to its right, hydrogen ion included, gets pulled back.
